title_en: Reply of the Supreme People's Court on the Issue of the Time Limit for a Party to Raise an Objection to Jurisdiction in Economic Dispute Cases

articles.content_en: 1. In a first-instance economic dispute case accepted by a People's Court, if a party raises an objection to the court's jurisdiction within the statutory defense period, the court shall first consider whether it has jurisdiction over the case; if the objection is raised after the expiration of the period, the court shall not consider it.

2. If a party raises an objection to the court's jurisdiction within the statutory defense period but, before the court renders a ruling on whether it has jurisdiction, expresses acceptance of the jurisdiction of the court accepting the case in written or oral form (which shall be recorded by the court and signed by the party), it shall be deemed that the party has voluntarily waived the objection. Thereafter, if the party raises a jurisdictional objection again during the litigation, the court shall not consider it.

3. After a ruling of the court of first instance or second instance rejecting a jurisdictional objection becomes legally effective, if a party petitions regarding the jurisdictional issue of the court, it shall not affect the court's adjudication of the case.

4. After a judgment rendered by the court on a case becomes legally effective, if a party petitions against both the ruling that rejected the jurisdictional objection and the judgment together, the court, after review, finding that although the jurisdiction is erroneous, the judgment is correct, shall not modify it; if upon review, it finds that both the jurisdiction and the judgment are indeed erroneous, it shall handle the case in accordance with the trial supervision procedure. If, after retrial or trial by a higher court, both the original judgment and ruling are set aside, the case shall be transferred to a People's Court with jurisdiction for adjudication.
August 5, 1990
